synopsis: Australia’s model WHS regulation 215 requires reasonably practicable control of collision risks and a warning device where collision is possible, but prescribes no automatic braking, test speed or distance; the model regulations operate only when adopted by a state or territory [f2254, f2255, f2257, f2256]. Canada is described as regulating mining province by province, with CSA M424 as the relevant national standard, but the booklet did not verify that standard or provincial regulations, found no federal collision-avoidance or automatic-braking rule, and recommends a province-by-province compliance matrix [f15525, f15528, f15526, f15529]. NSW braking guidance proposes service/secondary minimum mean net decelerations of 0.60/0.30 m/s² in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² in type testing, with grade and mass corrections; these are proposed values, not an adopted rule, qualifying passages that describe 0.60 m/s² as a requirement [f13946, f236, f5889]. Incident evidence shows continuing risk: NSW reported no meaningful year-on-year reduction in vehicle interactions in July 2023 and 30 underground-coal LHD/personnel-transport collisions over the 12 months to mid-2025, while Queensland ranked mobile-plant collisions highest among high-potential incidents in 2024 and warned of under-reporting [f3111, f3196, f3006, f3049]. Queensland guidance calls for foreseeable-scenario assessments and testing across objects and environmental conditions, warns that idealised detection zones can create false protection, and identifies QGN 33 as guidance rather than a Recognised Standard [f3603, f3600, f5753, f2268]. Australian state-specific collision-avoidance requirements were not found and should be checked before reliance; likewise, the Australian modifications to AS 21815.1:2023 were not accessible, and the listed standards are not law unless incorporated by a regulator or contract [f7501, f7502, f2260, f2263].
